transcript.content: Hey, what's going on guys? So we had a really good time at DevSecOps Days this past weekend. And I wanted to reach out and talk about it a little bit.

Yeah, for sure. We were talking earlier today about how the conference was going. It's always great to go and get exposed to some new ideas, meet other people, and just have that kind of community aspect. And I think it's important as well to just remind everybody that security is something that has to be a part of every development process.

Yeah, exactly. So for those who might not know what DevSecOps Days is, it was a conference in the greater DC area. And we had a lot of people from a bunch of different companies come together to talk about security and development and how they intersect.

Yeah, exactly. And I think one of the key takeaways for me was really just that there are so many different ways you can approach security in your development process. And it's not a one-size-fits-all solution, right? It depends on what type of application you're building, what language, and all those kinds of things.

Yeah, exactly. I had the opportunity to talk about some security best practices with some folks from Azure who were there. And they gave me a really good insight into their tooling as well. One thing that stuck out was how important it is for developers to have a strong security background.

Absolutely. I think one of the things we talked about was bringing in people who have a strong security background into development teams. Developers should not be expected to know everything about security; they can't possibly keep up with every new threat and vulnerability.

Yeah, that's so true. And I think it's really important for developers to understand the basics of security, but then also have someone on their team who is a security expert to help them out with any specific concerns or questions.

Exactly. And I think that brings us into our next topic: modernizing legacy applications. So you guys might remember from one of the episodes we did earlier, we talked a lot about updating old systems like the Lamp stack, which is what Apache, MySQL, PHP.

Exactly, exactly. And I think that's really important because these older stacks can be pretty vulnerable to new types of attacks. But it's a difficult process because you have to balance the need for security with the functionality and performance of your application.

Yeah, exactly. Sometimes you just have to hard left or hard right, meaning taking a stance and making significant changes rather than incremental improvements. It's not always easy, but it's necessary for modernizing applications.

Yeah, exactly. And one of the things that I found really interesting was how much the cloud service providers have changed over the years. For example, Azure used to be pretty confusing for me, but it has become a lot more user-friendly.
Yeah, absolutely. And Google Cloud Platform (GCP) is definitely the most intuitive design I've ever seen, but Azure has certainly improved over time as well.
Yeah, exactly. So when it comes to choosing between Azure, AWS, and GCP, which one would you recommend?
Well, I think that depends on the specific needs of your organization. But if we had to pick one, I'd probably go with Google Cloud Platform (GCP) because it's so easy to use and understand.

Yeah, definitely. And for those who might not know, DevSecOps Days is a conference that focuses on bringing together developers and security experts to discuss how to make software development more secure. And we had a really great time at this year's event.

Absolutely. And if you're interested in learning more about DevSecOps, we have some upcoming episodes lined up for the next few weeks where we'll be discussing various topics related to security and development.

summary: The conversation revolves around a project focused on tracking and analyzing illicit activities involving ships, particularly related to petroleum products and sanctions evasion. The speakers discuss various aspects such as ship transfers, risk assessments of ports, data sources, analysis methods, and potential commercial applications. Key points include the use of satellite imagery, AIS data, corporate records, and other geospatial technologies to identify suspicious activity. The project is led by C4ADS (Center for Civilians in Conflict), a non-profit organization specializing in sanctions evasion and illicit activities involving maritime trade.

key_points.point: Illicit ship-to-ship transfers of marine diesel occur in high-traffic areas like Singapore, where the large volume of transactions can mask illegal activity.
Ports most at risk for illicit activities include export locations (e.g., Card Islands) and centers of demand (e.g., East Asia).
Data sources used in the project include satellite imagery, AIS data, IHS market shipping records, and corporate records.
The process of analyzing a ship takes about 30 minutes to identify suspicious activity, followed by an additional six hours for building out the case study with supporting documents.
C4ADS is currently not using RF data but plans to incorporate it in the future to enhance tracking capabilities.
For Iran-specific projects, C4ADS primarily works with US government entities. For other regions like DPRK or Venezuela, they collaborate more extensively with international organizations.

title: Experimental Technology and Prehistory with Erik Nielsen
summary: In this episode, we delve into the fascinating world of experimental archaeology and prehistoric technology with Erik Nielsen, an expert in flint knapping and tool production. Erik shares his insights on the relevance of prehistory for modern humans, the challenges and rewards of creating replicas of ancient tools, and the importance of passing down these skills to future generations.

key_points.point: The significance of prehistoric technology in understanding human evolution
key_points.details: Erik explains how studying stone tool production helps us understand the development of human motoric scales, cognitive abilities, and cultural behaviors.

key_points.point: Relevance to modern society
key_points.details: Erik discusses how exploring our prehistoric past can help us better understand ourselves and the unity among all humans despite different customs and backgrounds.

key_points.point: Advice for aspiring experimental archaeologists
key_points.details: Erik emphasizes the importance of having a craft background, dedication, and asking experienced individuals for guidance. He also notes that age is not a barrier to learning these skills.

quotes: More and more we see this thing also with the astrogenetic research... I think it's important for us to understand where we come from and how we became human and how we started using tools.

I think that older people with no background in napping or archaeology can do this. If you really want to figure it out, it helps a lot if you're good at crafts and have like a little bit of an artistic side.

{{}}: What did you think of Batman Returns? Do you agree that the penguin's accent is terrible?
I thought it was pretty good, but I can see why someone might not like it. I don't think the penguin's accent was terrible though. It was just a bit over-the-top and cartoonish for my taste.
What were your favorite performances in Batman Returns? Do you agree that Michelle Fyfer's performance of Selena Kyle/Catwoman is better than Margot Robbie's?

My favorite performances were Christopher Walken as the Penguin, Dave Edwads as Harvey Dent, and Michelle Pfeiffer as Catwoman. I do think Michelle Pfeiffer's performance was better than Margot Robbie's.
What did you think of Batman's character development in this film? Do you agree that it could have been more explored?

I thought the character development for Batman wasn't as strong as it could have been. He seemed more like a supporting character to the villains and didn't get enough screen time with other characters.

summary:
The conversation delves into themes of redemption, grace, and love in Christian theology, emphasizing the importance of forgiveness and understanding for personal growth and community healing. Key points include:

1. **Judgment vs. Love**: The discussion contrasts judgment with God's loving approach to sinners, as seen through stories like that of the prodigal son and the woman caught in adultery.
2. **Personal Experience with Pornography**: Stephen shares his struggle with pornography and how seeking forgiveness and healing has impacted his ability to love others without condemnation.
3. **The Role of Healing in Love**: It is suggested that genuine love towards others can only come after one's own wounds are addressed through God’s grace and forgiveness.
4. **Exposure as a Pathway to Freedom**: The idea that facing and exposing past sins and hurts (including rejection) is necessary for true healing and freedom, leading to greater compassion toward others.
5. **Addressing Mental Health**: The hosts discuss the need to integrate discussions of mental health within the context of Christian theology, emphasizing God's love and willingness to heal even deeply rooted issues.
6. **Seeking Forgiveness and Love**: A call for individuals to seek forgiveness from God and one another, understanding that true freedom comes from acknowledging our sins and allowing God to forgive us.
7. **Community Healing**: The importance of a community that understands and practices forgiveness, love, and grace towards all members is highlighted as essential for collective spiritual growth and well-being.

title: Dealing with Racism and Its Impact: A Personal Reflection
transcript: The host discusses their personal experiences and reflections on racism, its impact on black individuals, and the need to find a balance between turning the other cheek and standing up for oneself. The podcast delves into the daily struggles faced by black people and how they are often affected by systemic issues. The host mentions George Floyd's death as a significant event that highlights the ongoing issue of police brutality against black individuals. They also touch on the impact of racism in public spaces, such as customers waving at them with a Trump visor or sign, and their reaction to these situations. Additionally, the host reflects on the values instilled by Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X, suggesting that black people should strive for nonviolent resistance while still being prepared to defend themselves. The podcast concludes with an acknowledgment of the complexities involved in addressing such issues and a commitment to continue the conversation.

Leaders making mistakes are normal; it's how they handle these situations that matters. Leaders can earn greater respect through genuine follow-up actions.

Summary: The conversation revolves around implementing COVID-19 safety measures in construction, particularly for painters. Key points include the challenges of convincing owners to invest in safety plans, creating an effective disciplinary system, and educating clients about the safety protocols in place. Participants discuss various aspects such as the size and content of safety plans, the importance of professional appearance, and customizing safety guidelines for specific projects. Overall, the focus is on providing practical guidance to help construction companies navigate this new landscape while maintaining a professional image.

Key Points.Safety Plan Implementation:
Many small construction companies lack existing safety programs, making it challenging to transition to new protocols.

Proper enforcement of rules and creating a culture of safety is difficult due to financial pressures and the desire to meet deadlines.
Key Points.Disciplinary Measures:
A step-by-step approach (verbal warning, written warning, day off, termination) can help enforce safety protocols effectively without being overly harsh or lenient.

Lack of discipline leads to complacency among workers, undermining efforts to improve safety standards.
Key Points.Client Education and Professionalism:
Educating clients about the safety measures in place enhances professionalism and trust. This includes explaining the behavior expected from both customers and workers when on-site.

Customizing safety plans for individual projects can provide a competitive edge by showing thorough preparation and commitment to safety.
Key Points.Safety Plan Content and Distribution:
A concise 18-page document is sufficient for most companies, with key categories like personal protective equipment (PPE), training, and emergency procedures being essential.

Providing the full plan or its table of contents on a company website can foster transparency and build trust among clients.
Key Points.Subcontractor Inclusion:
Subcontractors should be included in safety plans to ensure compliance across all parties involved in construction projects. Ignorance about safety protocols is seen as unacceptable and can jeopardize a company's reputation.

Customizing safety guidelines for subcontractors ensures that all workers adhere to the same standards, regardless of their official classification.
Key Points.Professionalism and Compliance:
Maintaining professional behavior on-site, including attire and adherence to protocols, contributes to the overall image of professionalism. This includes addressing issues like wearing masks properly and ensuring hands are clean before handling materials.

Customizing safety plans for specific projects can highlight a company's commitment to safety and professionalism.

title: The Five Key Qualities of an Awesome Mom

messageSummary.description: The first key quality of an awesome mom is unconditional love, which means not loving a child for what they can give to us but rather just for who they are. We need to be willing to give them what they need, even if it's not always what they want.

The second key quality is deep care, which involves caring for our children emotionally while also taking care of ourselves physically, mentally, and spiritually. We must prioritize self-care in order to be fully present for our families.

The third key quality is hope, a belief that there will always be a better tomorrow, no matter what today looks like. This sense of optimism can help us persevere through challenges and give our children a positive outlook on life.

The fourth key quality is prayer, surrendering the lives of our loved ones to God and trusting that He will provide for them in His perfect timing. This can help us maintain perspective during difficult times and seek guidance from above.

The final key quality is devotion to God, which means prioritizing our relationship with Him over other aspects of life. By focusing on Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior, we can model healthy relationships and gain wisdom for daily living.

closingPrayer: Thank you so much for the gift of motherhood. Help us to be loving, caring, hopeful, prayerful, and devoted mothers who reflect Your love in all our actions and words. In Jesus' name we pray, Amen.

title: Skate Talk with Andy Wagner from Sunshine Distribution - Razors Shift and Free Skates!
description: [UPBEAT MUSIC] [HOST (RYAN):] Hey there, guys! Welcome back to the channel. Today I have an amazing guest joining me for a skate talk. It's none other than Andy Wagner from Sunshine Distribution. We're going to dive into some of his new projects with Razors Skates and discuss what's next for the skating industry. This is a must-watch for anyone interested in the latest developments in roller sports. So, without further ado, let's jump right into it!]
transcript:
Hey there, everyone. I'm Ryan from Roller Skater Central, and today we're diving into an exciting interview with Andy Wagner from Sunshine Distribution. We'll be talking about some upcoming products like Razors' Shift skates and their new free skates. So let's get started.

[HOST (RYAN):] Alright, welcome to the channel. I'm Ryan from Roller Skater Central. And I am here today with Andy Wagner from Sunshine Distribution. Andy, thank you so much for taking the time to speak with me about your latest projects and some of your upcoming stuff that's going on right now.

[ANDY WAGNER]: Yeah, thanks for having me. So let’s get started. We’ve got a lot of things coming up. The first thing is Razors Shift Skates, which is our new inline skate. It came out in April and we’ve been working with it over the last few months, getting it to where it needs to be so that we can release it for 2024.

[RYAN]: That sounds great! Can you tell us more about this Shift skate?

[ANDY WAGNER]: So this is a hybrid. It's a free-ride and aggressive inline skates, which means it's going to be very versatile. But we are targeting the free-ride segment because that’s where most of our customer base is. There will definitely be an option for those who want more speed and performance in the future.

[RYAN]: That sounds really cool! And what about the new Razors free skates? When can we expect them to hit the market?

[ANDY WAGNER]: Well, it's going to be a while. We're still working on the molds. There’s been a lot of work and development that needs to go into making sure we have the best quality and design. We’ve put in about two years of research already, so there won't be any shortcuts.

[RYAN]: Got it! And what kind of new technologies are you guys looking at incorporating into these free skates?

[ANDY WAGNER]: Well, one thing is the boot molding. It's going to be completely new with a much better design and feel. We're also working on other areas like the frame and cup to make sure everything works together seamlessly.

[RYAN]: That sounds promising! And I know you mentioned that there will be an option for more speed in the future. Can you tell us anything about that?

[ANDY WAGNER]: Yeah, we're going to have a higher-end version of Shift, which is called ‘Razors Apex.’ We’re working on it right now and expect it out sometime next year.

[RYAN]: That's awesome! So for those who are interested in these new skates, what can they do to stay updated?

[ANDY WAGNER]: They can visit our website. We’ll have all the latest information there, including upcoming releases and product updates. And don't forget to follow us on social media!

[RYAN]: Great advice! So Andy, as you know, I've been following your career for a while now. I'm curious—why haven’t you ventured into anything related to roller skates before this?

[ANDY WAGNER]: Well, we started with inline skates because they are more versatile and cater better to the modern lifestyle. But as our company grows, we might explore other areas in the future if we find the right opportunities.

[RYAN]: That makes sense. And I heard John Hell was also working on something related to roller skates. Did you guys ever consider partnering with him?

[ANDY WAGNER]: We did look into it, but ultimately decided not to for a few reasons. We wanted to focus on inline skating first and ensure we were making quality products before branching out.

[RYAN]: I can see that being wise. So, what do you think the future holds for the roller sports industry as a whole?

[ANDY WAGNER]: I think it's going to continue to grow. With more people looking for ways to stay active and healthy, roller skating will definitely have its place in this market.

[RYAN]: Agreed! And with all these new products coming out, I'm excited to see what the future holds for Roller Skater Central as well. Thanks again, Andy, for your time and insights!

[ANDY WAGNER]: Thank you so much for having me. It was great chatting with you.

[RYAN]: You too! And that's it for today’s skate talk. I hope you guys found this informative and exciting. If you liked what you heard, don't forget to subscribe and hit the notification bell to stay updated on all our future content. Thanks again, and see you next time!

guest_info.name: Karen Chien
guest_info.title: Chief Innovation Officer at Autodesk, author of 'Start Within'
guest_info.expertise: Innovation, design thinking, and leading change within large organizations

topic_overview.topic: The importance of innovation in today's business environment
Leading change within large corporations without being a rogue cowboy
Prototyping and iteration as part of the creative process

showpoints.point: Karen discusses how traditional corporate structures can hinder true innovation, but emphasizes that it’s possible to work within those constraints.
showpoints.quote: "You're not a rogue cowboy, you're a creative artist, finding your way forward."

showpoints.point: Innovation should be seen as a process rather than an event or project.
showpoints.quote: "The little ideas tweaking your way forward can lead to the big innovation.",

showpoints.point: Prototyping and iteration are key components of bringing ideas to life, but must also involve constructive feedback from others.
showpoints.quote: "You're not only allowing the idea to evolve, but you're also teaching others how to be constructive and giving feedback."

showpoints.point: The book 'Start Within' by Karen Chien is a practical guide for anyone looking to innovate within their organization or as an individual.
showpoints.quote: "It's not just about the perfect linear way forward, but about dipping in and unlocking those moments of change."

showpoints.point: Leadership plays a crucial role in creating a culture that supports innovation.
showpoints.quote: "One of the biggest things holding people back is the word 'innovation' - it's super exclusive sounding, and you don't associate with those words."

showpoints.point: The concept of 'vesting assumptions' introduced by Karen as a tool for fostering innovation within organizations.
showpoints.quote: "It's about getting out there, prototyping, and making those small steps."

conclusion.guest_thanks: Thank you to our guest, Karen Chien, for sharing her insights on innovation, leadership, and the creative process.

Title: Cassandra McKinley: The Fearless Vocalist and Educator

Questions.Question: How has your background as a music educator influenced your approach to performing and teaching?
Questions.Answer: As a music educator, I've always believed that the learning process is cyclical. It's not just about imparting knowledge but also receiving it. In my performances, I try to connect with my audience in a way that fosters an understanding of music and its cultural significance. Teaching helps me see where gaps exist and how we can bridge them through performance.

Questions.Question: Your music blends jazz, soul, and country influences. Can you explain the creative process behind your latest album?
Questions.Answer: My latest album is a reflection of my journey as an artist. It draws from various genres because I believe that music should be free and diverse. Each song tells a story or evokes an emotion. The blend of jazz, soul, and country is not just for the sake of it; it's about exploring different emotions and experiences.

Questions.Question: You've had to overcome many challenges in your career. How do you maintain resilience?
Questions.Answer: Resilience comes from recognizing that setbacks are opportunities for growth. I remind myself that every challenge is a stepping stone towards becoming a better artist and human being. I keep moving forward, learning from each experience, and never giving up on my dreams.

Questions.Question: What advice would you give to someone who aspires to be both a musician and an educator?
Questions.Answer: Embrace the diversity of your experiences. As a musician, you're an artist; as an educator, you're a mentor. Combine these roles by being passionate, patient, and open-minded. Always seek to inspire others and foster a love for music that can last a lifetime.

Questions.Question: How do you balance your solo career with teaching and coaching?
Questions.Answer: Balancing multiple roles requires discipline and prioritization. I make sure to set clear boundaries between work and personal time. Teaching and coaching allow me to interact closely with students, which informs my music and vice versa. It's a symbiotic relationship that keeps me grounded and inspired.

Without further ado, let’s dive into our conversation with Jotem McKinney.
LaToya: Hello, Jotem! Welcome back to the podcast. How are you doing today?
Jotem: Hey LaToya! I'm good. Thank you for having me. I’m excited about this conversation.

LaToya: Yes, we are too! First of all, thank you so much for sharing your story and your experiences with us. For our listeners who might not be familiar with The Breathing Room, can you tell them a little bit about it?

Jotem: Absolutely! The Breathing Room is a platform I created to provide a safe space for women. It's essentially a community where we can come together and share our truths, our struggles, and also celebrate the beauty of motherhood. So many times in the body of Christ, there are stigmatized topics that are not talked about openly because of shame or guilt, like postpartum depression, anxiety, and other things. The Breathing Room is a place where women can come together, relax, let it all out, and just be themselves.
LaToya: That's wonderful! Can you tell us more about your journey as a mother? How did you find yourself in this role, and what challenges have you faced along the way?

Jotem: Thank you for asking. Motherhood is such an amazing experience but it's not without its struggles. I had my first child when I was 28 years old. It was beautiful but also challenging. The whole process of becoming a mother, from the pre-pregnancy stage to postpartum, there are so many things that happen in between that you really don't expect or know how to handle. For instance, during pregnancy, my husband and I were going through some marital issues which made it hard for me to fully enjoy being pregnant because of all those other things going on.
LaToya: That sounds like a lot to juggle. How did that affect you emotionally and mentally?

Jotem: It was very overwhelming, and honestly, it contributed to the postpartum depression I experienced. After she was born, I felt so much pressure from society, church, family, and even myself, to be this perfect mom. And when you're dealing with that kind of pressure, combined with everything else going on in life, it's really tough. The first year of motherhood was very hard for me because I was also trying to balance my career as a teacher while taking care of our little one. But the most challenging part, for sure, was the postpartum depression.
LaToya: That must have been incredibly difficult. Can you tell us more about your experience with postpartum depression?

Jotem: Yes, it was really tough. For a long time, I thought my feelings were normal and that everyone else just had an easier time with motherhood. But when the thoughts of suicide started to creep in, I knew something wasn't right. I went through counseling and medication, but even then, the emotions would come back and hit me hard. It was a dark place for a while, and I felt so alone. So many women go through it and don’t talk about it because there's still stigma around mental health in the church.
LaToya: That’s really important to bring attention to. It can be so isolating when you’re dealing with postpartum depression, especially if you feel like you're not supposed to share your struggles.

Jotem: Exactly! I think it's crucial for women to talk about these things and seek help, whether that means talking to a therapist or just sharing their experiences in a safe space. The Breathing Room is one such place where we can do that.
LaToya: So, you mentioned creating The Breathing Room as a platform to share your story and the stories of other women. What inspired you to start this project?

Jotem: Well, it all started when I had my first child. At the time, there was no space for women who were going through similar experiences. So many times, women feel like they have to hide their struggles or pretend everything is perfect. But that's not real life! I wanted a place where women could come and just be themselves without fear of judgment. The Breathing Room provides that kind of environment – a safe space for women to share their truths.
LaToya: That’s amazing! And how has the response been so far?

Jotem: It's been really encouraging. Women have been reaching out and sharing their stories, and it's created such a sense of community. Some of them are going through postpartum depression or other mental health issues, but they feel like they're not alone anymore. They see that there are others who understand what they’re going through.
LaToya: That’s wonderful to hear! Moving on, you also recently launched your own personal brand called Just Jutem. Can you tell us more about this and why it's important for you?

Jotem: Sure thing! The idea behind the name 'Just Jutem' is that I want people to see me as an individual first. Too often, women are defined by their roles in society – mom, wife, teacher, pastor’s wife. But who am I beyond those titles? The answer is just me, Jotem McKinney. I wanted a brand where I can share my story and experiences without the pressure of being labeled or boxed into these specific roles.
LaToya: That's really powerful! And you’re also working on some upcoming projects like a devotional book for new moms. Can you tell us more about that?

Jotem: Yes, I am! The devotional book is aimed at helping new moms navigate the challenges of motherhood while finding strength in their faith. It will be a combination of scripture, personal anecdotes, and practical advice. I want to provide comfort and encouragement for those who feel overwhelmed or unsure about their roles as mothers.
LaToya: That sounds like such an important resource! And on that note, where can our listeners find you online? Do they have any way to connect with you?

Jotem: Yes, definitely. You can follow me and The Breathing Room on Instagram (@love.me.jetaimed) and Facebook (justjutemofficial). I’m always open to connecting and providing support for new moms who might need it.

LaToya: Thank you so much, Jotem, for sharing your story with us today. Your courage and dedication to creating a space where women can breathe and be themselves is truly inspiring. We appreciate you being here!
Jotem: Thank you, LaToya! It's been an honor to share this journey with you.

LaToya: And thank you to all our listeners for tuning in. If you’d like to join the conversation or connect with Jotem and The Breathing Room, make sure to follow us on social media. Until next time, remember that God has a beautiful plan for each of us.

title: Let's Connect - Episode 16: G & Keith on Spirituality, Connection, and Transformation
transcript:
Host: Hello everyone, welcome to another episode of the Let’s Connect podcast. I’m your host, Keith.

In today’s episode, we have a special guest with us - G. G is a transformational coach who has been my guide and mentor on my personal journey towards spiritual growth. We are going to dive into some deep topics such as the nature of spirituality, connection, and transformation. So let's get started.

G: Hi everyone, it's really great to be here with you today. Thank you for having me on this episode.

Host: G, can you tell us a bit about yourself and your journey?

G: Of course! I'm a transformational coach based in Los Angeles. My path has been one of self-discovery and learning to connect with the spiritual aspects of life. I believe that we are all spiritual beings having a human experience, and my goal is to help others find their highest selves.

Host: That's amazing! Can you explain what transformational coaching means to you?

G: Transformational coaching is about helping clients unlock their potential for growth by exploring the root causes of limiting beliefs and behaviors. The goal is to empower them to take action towards achieving their goals.

Host: Can you share a little bit about your coaching methods?

G: Sure! I use techniques like meditation, visualization, and energy work to help clients tap into their inner wisdom. We also explore the concept of the higher self, which is essentially our true essence or divine nature.

Host: How do you see the relationship between spirituality and transformational coaching?

G: Spirituality is at the core of transformational coaching. It provides a framework for understanding ourselves on a deeper level, allowing us to make positive changes in our lives.

Host: You mentioned the higher self earlier. Can you elaborate more on that?

G: The higher self is our divine essence or true nature. It's the part of us that connects us to the universe and allows us to tap into wisdom and intuition.

Host: That's fascinating! How does one connect with their higher self?

G: Connecting with the higher self involves practices like meditation, journaling, and spending time in nature. It’s about being present and allowing oneself to be guided by inner wisdom.

Host: G, you've spoken a lot about transformational coaching and spirituality. Can you share an experience that has deeply impacted your journey?

G: One of the most impactful experiences for me was when I coached someone to discover their highest self. They envisioned themselves as a bright light and going back to nature, and it changed the way they viewed themselves and their place in the world.

Host: Wow, that sounds incredibly powerful! How do you see your role as a coach?

G: As a coach, my job is to evoke transformation. I provide guidance and support, but ultimately it's the client who does the work.

Host: That's such an important distinction. Can you tell us about your upcoming plans?

G: Absolutely! We are planning a retreat in Maui next February where I will host my first retreat. It’s going to be a beautiful place, perfect for connecting with nature and the divine.

Host: Wow, that sounds incredible. How do you stay connected to your own spirituality?

G: For me, staying connected involves being fully present in the moment and not overthinking or over-feeling. It's about embodying the present.

Host: G, it has been such a pleasure speaking with you today. Thank you for sharing your insights and wisdom with us.

G: Thank you, Keith! It’s always a joy to connect with you and share these ideas. I hope our listeners found this episode enlightening as well.
summary: In this episode of Let's Connect, Keith interviews G, a transformational coach based in Los Angeles. They discuss the nature of spirituality, connection, and transformation. G shares their journey and how they use techniques like meditation, visualization, and energy work to help clients tap into their inner wisdom. The conversation also delves into the concept of the higher self and its role in personal growth. G talks about a powerful experience where coaching someone led them to discover their highest self. The episode concludes with plans for an upcoming retreat in Maui.

guest_interviews.question: What are your thoughts on the overall sound and atmosphere of 'Cowboys from Hell'? How does it compare to Pantera's previous work?
guest_interviews.answer: 'Cowboys from Hell' is a really tough, hard-hitting record. It’s definitely in that groove metal vein, but it has its own distinct flavor compared to their earlier works. The production is thicker and more intense, which is fitting for the album's darker themes.

guest_interviews.question: Can you tell us about some of your favorite tracks on 'Cowboys from Hell'?
guest_interviews.answer: Definitely 'Patched Up', 'Wolverine', and 'Dysrhythmia'. 'Wolverine' has a really heavy, almost industrial feel to it. 'Dysrhythmia' is just a classic Pantera track with its tight riffs and aggressive vocals.

guest_interviews.question: How did the creative process for this album differ from previous projects?
guest_interviews.answer: The band had been working on this material for a while, and we wanted to capture a more mature sound. The production was a bit different too; it’s thicker and more polished compared to some of their earlier stuff.

guest_interviews.question: What specific techniques or equipment did you use in the studio that contributed to the overall sound of 'Cowboys from Hell'?
guest_interviews.answer: We used a lot of compression and distortion to get those thick, heavy sounds. Also, the guitar cabinets were really important; we built custom ones with extra low-end to capture the aggression of the music.

guest_interviews.question: How did your vocal approach change for this album compared to previous work?
guest_interviews.answer: For 'Cowboys from Hell', I wanted a more aggressive and in-your-face sound. We recorded all the vocals live, which gave it that raw energy. It was really important to capture that intensity.

guest_interviews.question: Can you discuss the impact of 'Cowboys from Hell' on both the heavy metal scene and your personal journey as an artist?
guest_interviews.answer: 'Cowboys from Hell' was a significant album for us, it pushed the boundaries of what we could do musically. It had a huge impact on the metal scene and really defined Pantera's sound in the '90s. As an artist, it taught me a lot about pushing myself creatively.

# Podcast Episode Transcription
## [00:03:18] - Swayze
Swayze: Hi guys, and welcome back to the #TrueSex podcast. I'm so excited to have with us today, Rachel, Whitney Miller's amazing partner in crime. She's someone who has inspired me so much over these past few months that I can't help but reach out and say, let's be friends, let's chat, and I think it was totally worth it because she's absolutely brilliant.

## [00:03:46] - Whitney
Whitney: Hi Swayze. Hey, how are you doing?
Swayze: Hey there. Doing good. So, we're both so excited to be here and kind of share this conversation that we've had about the True Sex podcast.

## [00:03:56] - Whitney
Whitney: Yeah, yeah, I'm really excited to chat with you as well. It's great to hear from you again.
Swayze: And thanks for the shout out, and also for your kind words about True Sex Podcast in the past, so thank you for that.

## [00:04:07] - Swayze
Swayze: I just think it's so amazing what you're doing. You know? I feel like there's this movement or this community of folks who are really getting into a space where they can be open and honest, and I think that's such an important part of the world right now.

## [00:04:23] - Whitney
Whitney: Yeah. It is important for sure. And it's important to have those conversations in a way that feels safe, that feels like you can really speak freely and express yourself without feeling judged or being put down. I think that's the essence of what we're doing here on True Sex.

## [00:04:39] - Swayze
Swayze: Yeah, totally. And as a listener, when it comes to podcasts, I'm looking for a really deep dive into conversations, and I think you guys are providing that.
Whitney, can you tell us a bit about the True Sex podcast? What's your mission or what's the purpose behind it?

## [00:04:53] - Whitney
Whitney: Yeah. So for me, it started with the True Love Podcast as well, which is a sister show to this. The purpose there was to create a space where we could have open and honest conversations about relationships and sex, but also a little bit of self-care and how that all intersects.

## [00:05:09] - Swayze
Swayze: Yeah. And it's not just like a one-way conversation; you guys are really engaging your audience in the process as well, right?
Whitney: Absolutely. I mean, we love having guests who can share their stories and experiences with us, but also, we have a ton of listeners on our True Love Podcast who contribute to the show by sending in questions or sharing their own experiences.

## [00:05:26] - Whitney
Whitney: And so it's that collaborative space where people can come and feel like they're part of something, and we're creating this community. That's really what I love about it the most is that aspect of building a community.

## [00:05:37] - Swayze
Swayze: And you mentioned earlier True Love Podcast. Can you tell us a bit more about that, and how it relates to the True Sex podcast?
Whitney: Yeah, so True Love is kind of our sister show and we do episodes where we have guests or sometimes just two of us, where we talk about different relationship topics, but also there are episodes where we dive into things like masturbation, consent, and sex positivity. So it's really a space that covers all aspects of relationships and love.

## [00:05:59] - Swayze
Swayze: And then with the True Sex Podcast, what kind of topics or themes do you usually cover?
Whitney: With True Sex, we focus specifically on sex, pleasure, and intimacy. We want to make sure that people feel empowered to talk about these topics without any shame or stigma. Some recent episodes have included discussions around sex workers' rights, gender and sexuality, and even body image.

## [00:06:17] - Swayze
Swayze: That's amazing. And I think it really shows that you're creating a safe space for people to learn more about these topics and have those conversations in a way that they might not feel comfortable doing otherwise.
Whitney, can you share some of the most memorable moments or experiences from your podcast? Any highlights?

## [00:06:31] - Whitney
Whitney: Oh, wow. There are so many, but one episode in particular that comes to mind is when we had our guests who are sex workers. I think it was so powerful because these individuals were sharing their stories and experiences, which can be really vulnerable for them.

## [00:06:43] - Swayze
Swayze: That sounds incredible. And how do you handle the feedback or reactions that people might have to some of the more sensitive topics?
Whitney: We try our best to provide a platform where everyone can express themselves, but we also remind them that it's important to be respectful and considerate in their responses.

## [00:06:57] - Swayze
Swayze: And what do you think is the most important thing for people to take away from your podcast?
Whitney: I think the most important takeaway is that we all have unique experiences and stories when it comes to sex, relationships, and our bodies. It's about embracing those differences and finding ways to connect with others despite them.

## [00:07:13] - Swayze
Swayze: Beautiful. And on that note, is there anything you'd like to add or any future plans for the podcast?
Whitney: Yeah, we're always looking to expand our guest list and bring in more diverse voices. We also have some exciting new topics we want to explore, including non-binary identities and kink communities.

## [00:07:28] - Swayze
Swayze: Sounds fantastic. And for anyone who hasn't listened yet, where can they find True Sex Podcast?
Whitney: You can find us on Spotify, Apple Podcasts, Google Podcasts, and pretty much all the major podcast directories.

## [00:07:38] - Swayze
Swayze: Great. Well, Whitney, it's been such a pleasure chatting with you today. I'm looking forward to listening more of your episodes in the future and seeing where this amazing journey takes you.
Whitney: Thank you so much for having me. It was great talking to you as well.

poem.title: Sedicated to George Floyd, Jamar Clark, Trayvon Martin, Sandra Bland, Brianna
poem.author: Ani Sivakumar
content: Sedicated to George Floyd, Jamar Clark, Trayvon Martin, Sandra Bland, Brianna, and then countless other names that did not deserve to be cut short.

And on behalf of my ancestors as a white human, as a white feminine human, working to deeply connect to Mother Earth and Mama Gaia and deeply touch the deep wounds that absolutely must be addressed at this time.
poem.purpose: To honor the victims of racial injustice and acknowledge personal responsibility in addressing systemic issues.

secondPoem.title: Equitable Sovereignty
secondPoem.author: Ani Sivakumar
content: Equitable sovereignty is a concept that takes you into your roots that uplifts and centers currently in previously marginalized groups.
Step up into voicing the parts of yourself that have been silenced because we change the fabric of the system when we go inside and tend to our inner landscape.
True equitable sovereignty means that all receive what they need. True equitable power is in womb wisdom.
secondPoem.purpose: To propose a new framework for social justice that emphasizes interconnectedness, healing, and empowerment.

transcription:
Hello everyone. Today we have an interesting episode with Larry, our guest who has shared some fascinating insights on being a sanitation worker during the pandemic and his experience of life in general. Let's dive right into it.

Larry started by sharing how his job as a sanitation worker has been incredibly demanding due to the pandemic. With the increase in waste production, his team had to work overtime to keep up with the demand. He mentioned that they now clean the streets more frequently and handle garbage twice as much as before. Larry shared that his work has become even more challenging due to the additional safety measures such as wearing masks, gloves, and sanitizers throughout their shifts.

Larry also discussed the impact of the pandemic on his mental health and how it has affected him both personally and professionally. He mentioned feeling a sense of urgency and stress in managing the increased waste volume while keeping himself and others safe. The financial strain due to job loss or reduced income has been another factor contributing to his anxiety.

Moving on, we talked about Larry's relationship with his siblings. He shared that they are supportive but can also be petty at times. Larry expressed how important it is for people to have a support system during tough times, and he feels fortunate to have such a dynamic family. His siblings are even eager to participate in his podcast, which shows their commitment and love.

Larry then shared an anecdote about a theory he had: that video gamers who play zombie games would be the best candidates for survival during a zombie apocalypse because they already have experience dealing with the unknown and unpredictable situations. This interesting observation sparked some discussions among our listeners as well.

Lastly, we touched upon Larry's personal projects and aspirations. He expressed his desire to learn more about music and mentioned that he is working on marketing plans for an upcoming video project with a friend named Mariah Escal. It seems like Larry is using this platform not only to share his experiences but also as a means of self-expression in the realm of music.

In conclusion, today's episode has given us a glimpse into the life of a sanitation worker during these unprecedented times and how personal challenges can shape one's perspective on various aspects of life. Thank you for listening, and we hope you found Larry's story inspiring. Stay tuned for our next episode where we will explore more interesting topics with diverse guests.

introduction: Welcome to Beer & Bread, the show where we dive into everything beer and bread. I'm your host, [Host Name], and today we have a special episode featuring You Into Beer with Micky from HopCarts Out.
Before we get started, thanks for tuning in, guys! We appreciate you spending time with us. If you enjoy the show, don't forget to subscribe, rate, and review us wherever you listen.
segment_1: Today, we're talking about You Into Beer's year-round selection of beers, including their Crooked Line Pale Ale, Black Lager, and other seasonal releases.

Micky from HopCarts Out shared some interesting details on these brews. For example, the Dooby IPA, which was originally a limited release but has since become part of their year-round lineup due to its popularity.
segment_2: But that's not all we're talking about today. We've got murder hornets on our mind, and no, I'm not talking about the TV show.
The Asian Giant Hornet, also known as the 'murder hornet,' is an invasive species from Asia with a reputation for decapitating honeybees in their hives. Can you imagine that? That's just... insane.
But there's hope! Japanese honey bees have evolved to fight back against these hornets by surrounding them and cooking them alive in a ball of their own bodies. Talk about teamwork!
segment_3: So, why hasn't this made the national news? Beats me. I mean, that's some serious stuff, right?

And to make matters even more interesting, there have been reports of beekeepers getting stung multiple times by these hornets while trying to fight them off. Just saying, if you're a beekeeper, maybe stick to honey?
segment_4: Anyway, back to the topic at hand – You Into Beer's offerings. They distribute to 32 states, so if you can't find their beers in your local store, check out their tap room or online options.
Thanks again to Micky for sending us some beautiful pictures of his glassware and supporting the show.
conclusion: That's all for today. If you have any questions or comments about You Into Beer or murder hornets (or both), feel free to reach out in the comments section below or via email.
Stay tuned for Round 21 when we turn the legal drinking age, and remember, always drink responsibly.

title: Potty Training Struggles and Lessons Learned
content:
The author shares her experience with potty training three of her four children, focusing on the struggles she faced with one of her daughters. She highlights the importance of understanding that every child is unique and may not follow a typical development path, emphasizing the need to give oneself grace during this challenging time.

Key takeaways:
- Potty training can be difficult for some children, even if others in your family are quick to succeed.
- Every child's experience with potty training will be different.
- Comparing your child's progress to other kids or even your own other children can be unhelpful and unnecessary.
- Understanding that milestones are guidelines, not hard-and-fast rules, can provide relief during vaccination appointments and well-child checkups.

The author also discusses the advice given by a urologist regarding her daughter Scarlet's potty training struggles. They suggested strategies such as ensuring full undressing or sitting backwards to fully empty bladders, and taking low-dose laxatives to help with urinary retention at night.

Overall, the lesson is that patience and self-compassion are crucial when navigating challenges in parenting.

summary: Sabrina Urban, a mom of four, shares her experience and insights about having a big family on the podcast 'Join Your Circus.' She talks about both the pros and cons of having multiple children. Some positive aspects include increased pride in seeing kids grow up and develop new skills, more frequent opportunities for bonding with each child, and being able to share the joy of parenthood with her partner. However, she also acknowledges challenges such as constantly being tired due to lack of sleep, difficulties watching TV together because of differing interests, struggling with names in moments of trouble, and the financial burden of childcare costs. Despite these challenges, Sabrina emphasizes that adding another child after having three didn't make a significant difference for her family. She concludes by encouraging people not to judge parents who choose to have large families and challenging listeners to offer genuine support when seeing them struggle.

title: Unhurry Light #403: Karen Rupp - Homebody Entrepreneur
transcript:
Jen: Welcome to episode 403 of Unhurry Light, where we have a wonderful chat with Karen Rupp. I'm Jen Brazil and today is September 19th, 2018.

Karen and I are long-time friends. We've known each other since our college days and both work in the same city now. She was kind enough to come over for a visit at my house this week as she's visiting family and we were able to chat about her journey of going from homebody photographer to businesswoman, and how it all started with a church group called Pursuit.

Jen: So let me introduce Karen Rupp. She is the founder of JLR Photography, which is a lifestyle photography company based in Chicago, Illinois. Karen also founded the business blogging platform called The Pursuit Project as well as the podcast with the same name. Karen was born and raised in Illinois. She has two beautiful children, Ava and Isaac. And she earned her Bachelor's degree from Northern Illinois University.

Karen: Hello Jen!

Jen: Hi, Karen! I'm so happy to have you on the show today. It's great that we finally had a chance to chat. So you know what? We'll just jump right in because it's been so many years since I've known you and really want to get started with your story. So why don't you tell us about where you're from, how you grew up, and how you became interested in photography?

Karen: Well, my hometown is a small town called Princeton, Illinois. We live just outside of Peoria. I was born here and raised here. My dad worked for a local factory until he retired, and my mom stayed home with us. The summers were great because we could go fishing, boating, swimming, and all the fun stuff that comes along with having a lake in your backyard! My family is very creative. We all love music, art, dance, drama, singing... So I was pretty young when I started taking photos, maybe 10 or 12, but my first camera wasn't until I was 16.

Jen: Did you always want to be a photographer?

Karen: Well, yes and no. When I first got the camera in high school, it was more of an experiment. I took pictures at football games and proms for fun but then my junior year of high school, my photography teacher put on a demonstration about taking senior portraits for high school students. I just fell in love with how much effort went into each session and how many photos the professional photographer would take to get one perfect photo. I was determined to make that career, even though it wasn't an easy thing to do.

Jen: Did you face any obstacles?

Karen: Yeah, actually. My parents were really worried about me taking up a business where I'd be outside all the time and not getting enough done in school. They felt that was going to have a negative impact on my grades. So it took a lot of conversation with them before they finally agreed for me to take the photography classes.

Jen: How did you balance your photography business while also taking care of family obligations?

Karen: I think I always put too much pressure on myself and never felt like there was enough time in the day. It's definitely a tough balancing act, but I worked hard when my kids were at school and then tried to take a break from it all once they got home.

Jen: How did you get into blogging?

Karen: Well, about 10 years ago, I started a blog with my best friend's husband. I wanted a place where we could share our experiences as business owners and mommas. Then one day in the summer of 2015, my friend suggested that I start writing down everything I learned on my own blog. So I did just that, but it really didn't get off to the best start because I was so busy with my photography business.

Jen: What led you to create a platform for other mommies to share their experiences as well?

Karen: I had already started a group called Pursuit on Facebook. It's just moms that want to run a home-based business and also be good moms. We all have the same goals, but we don't know how to reach them or if it's possible for us to do both at once. So we all started sharing our stories and tips as well.

Jen: How did you get into podcasting?

Karen: Well, I was already a blogger, so when my friend asked me if I wanted to be on the podcast she was creating, it just seemed like an easy transition. We're also both moms and business owners, so we definitely had that in common.

Jen: What inspired you to create The Pursuit Project platform?

Karen: Well, about 10 years ago, I was reading a book on the art of saying no by Laura Vanderkam. I started thinking about how often I said yes when what I really needed to do was say no. I realized that I wanted to make sure that The Pursuit Project would help people learn to set boundaries and find their balance in life.

Jen: What were some challenges you faced as a homebody entrepreneur?

Karen: There are so many! For one, it can be hard to feel like you have purpose. But I know now that God has given me this work for a reason and that's how I find my purpose each day.

Jen: Can you tell us more about your book, Homebody Entrepreneur?

Karen: Well, the book is all about taking a business you love to do at home and making it into something profitable. It covers so many different areas from marketing yourself as a professional, to understanding how to make money online, to managing your time well.

Jen: What advice would you give to someone who wants to start their own business?

Karen: Start small. It can be overwhelming and scary when you're just starting out, so take it slow and see where God leads you.

Jen: Karen, thank you for sharing your story with us today!

Karen: Thank you Jen! I've really enjoyed this conversation.

><!-- --><![CDATA[该对话讨论了多个话题，主要包括关于警察暴力和.content: <![CDATA[噫嘻，吾乃吴邪也，闲来无事之时，乐为君言音频节目之趣闻。今日所谈，乃一播客节目中关于洛杉矶市惠提尔区和平抗议活动的记录与观察。此节目名为《惠提尔之声》，由主持人Woody主持并分享其亲身经历与感想。'噫嘻，吾辈且听其详述。'噫嘻，吾今将向君细述其内容。'噫嘻，吾今述及者乃洛杉矶市惠提尔区之和平抗议活动。'据其言，此次抗议活动发生在6月4日，地点位于San Agustine大道与Whittier Boulevard交汇处，即惠提尔市的东区，该地区以白人和西班牙裔居民为主，被认为是上层社会区域。'吾今见其描述，此地之和平抗议活动似乎并未出现警察干涉，仅有一小部分人员在场指导参与者行进路线。参与者们举着标语，高呼口号，在San Agustine大道与Pascot街之间来回步行半英里左右的距离。'吾且言及一位女参与者所说之事，她表示Trader Joe超市向抗议者提供了整箱水，此乃一大善举。'然而，惠提尔市的和平抗议活动与上周日深夜在伍迪德地区的示威有所不同。据其言，上周日的抗议更具有攻击性，并且有更多年轻人和家庭参与其中，而这次则以孩子、家庭为主。值得注意的是，此次活动中有不少白人居民也表达了他们的观点。'吾辈可闻其言，曰：“种族主义不仅仅是白人的问题。”种族主义可以表现为任何人的问题。吾曾亲眼所见各种形式的歧视。因此，吾坚信，无论种族为何，人们都应该平等地对待他人。'吾辈且听其描述，抗议者们对于警方和正义制度有何诉求？据其所言，他们希望重新评估某些社区中的警官选拔标准以及警民关系。他指出如果警员无法理解和尊重所在社区，则不应分配到该区域工作。'此外，他还提到了1992年因罗德尼·金事件引发的洛杉矶暴动历史，并表示现在的抗议活动虽然与过去有所不同，但同样具有重要意义。'吾辈且听其言，“我们不能让我们的房子着火。”他呼吁人们不要破坏财产，而是通过和平集会表达自己的诉求。'然而，他也承认有些人可能只是利用这些机会获取一些他们本不属于的东西或进行不当行为，例如抢劫商店等。'噫嘻，吾今总结之，此音频节目分享了关于洛杉矶惠提尔区和平抗议活动的观察和感受，并回顾了1992年罗德尼·金事件引发的暴动历史。主持人通过实地考察与参与者交谈的方式记录了这些事件，并表达了对和平示威的支持以及对于种族主义的看法。'噫嘻，吾今告君，此节目名为《惠提尔之声》，由Woody主持并分享其亲身经历与感想。',

Key Messages: Maintain perspective on material things: It's important to not get overly emotional or upset about small material possessions like broken dishes or stained clothes. These can be replaced and dwelling on them isn't productive.
Focus on making smart, positive decisions: Quitting a job without another lined up is an irrational decision. It's better to find a new job that you enjoy and aligns with your goals.

Avoid illegal activities as a short-term fix: Selling drugs may provide quick money but can lead to serious legal issues and long-term consequences. It’s better to work hard, save money and make good choices.

Understand the impact of decisions on life outcomes: Good decisions can have positive long-term effects while bad ones will eventually catch up with you. Take your actions seriously and consider their full impacts.

Personal perspective is shaped by environment and upbringing: Our beliefs and behaviors are influenced by our surroundings, family, media, culture, etc. Acknowledge that others may see things differently due to their unique experiences.
Main Points: It's important not to dwell on minor material losses or imperfections. They can be replaced.

Making rational decisions is crucial: Quitting a job without another one lined up could lead to financial instability and hardship, especially during times of high unemployment like during the pandemic.

Illegal activities such as drug dealing are generally harmful and should be avoided; even if they seem like a quick fix. They can have long-term negative consequences including legal troubles and loss of personal freedom.
The decisions we make today shape our future. Positive choices lead to positive outcomes, while bad decisions may come back to haunt us later in life.
People's viewpoints vary based on their unique backgrounds and experiences. Understanding this diversity is important when giving or receiving advice.
Call to Action: Reflect on your own actions and decisions. Are they aligning with your long-term goals? If not, consider making changes now before it's too late.
Seek out positive influences in your life that can help guide you toward better choices.
Be open to the idea that others may see things differently from you due to their unique backgrounds and experiences.

podcastTitle: Episode #127: Andrew Serious on Good Stewards Podcast and More
transcriptionSummary: In this episode of the BiggerPockets Podcast, Brett Krock interviews Andrew Serious, co-founder and CEO of Stewardship Properties. They discuss the Good Stewards podcast, investing in houses versus apartment complexes, building a platform with a personal blog and social media presence, and more.
transcript:
Transcript:

[0:00] Brett Krock: Welcome to the BiggerPockets Podcast. I'm your host, Brett Krock. We have an amazing episode for you today featuring our friend, Andrew Serious, co-founder of the Good Stewards Podcast and CEO of Stewardship Properties. We discuss a lot of topics from his experience in real estate investing, including what he's seen changing over time with the markets and people and the differences between investing in houses versus apartment complexes. We also talk about building a platform through blogging, social media presence, and the Good Stewards Podcast. Andrew gives us some great insights into how to approach real estate investing and build your network, as well as his advice for our audience on how to get started. So, let's jump right in.

[0:45] Brett Krock: Hey, Andrew, welcome to the BiggerPockets Podcast.

[0:48] Andrew Serious: Thanks for having me, Brett. I'm excited to be here.

[0:51] Brett Krock: Yeah, thanks so much for joining us today and taking some time out of your schedule. I know you're a very busy man. So let's get started with the Good Stewards Podcast, which you host along with your dad and co-founders Ryan and Amanda. What has been the biggest takeaway or lesson that you've learned from hosting this podcast?

[1:06] Andrew Serious: Well, one of the big things I've learned is just that there are so many nuances to real estate investing beyond just buying a house at 45% of its appraised value and making some cash on it. It's really important to know your numbers, understand the market, have a solid plan in place, and be willing to stick with it through thick and thin. I think that's something we've seen time and time again from our guests as well as from our own experiences.

[1:29] Brett Krock: That makes so much sense. And what about the difference between investing in houses versus apartment complexes? You mentioned that you have a particular focus on smaller houses, but is there ever an instance where you see yourself moving into bigger multifamily properties?

[1:43] Andrew Serious: Yeah, we're definitely open to it. I think the challenge right now for us is just the market. It's kind of tough finding deals in apartment complexes that make sense given where we are and what our goals are with the company. But you know, one day, who knows? We might get into larger properties, but for now, houses definitely seem to be where we're focusing.

[2:05] Brett Krock: And it sounds like you've built out a great platform through your personal blog, social media presence, and the Good Stewards Podcast. What are some key things that you've learned about building a platform and how do you recommend our audience build their own platforms?

[2:17] Andrew Serious: Well, I think it's important to have a consistent message and voice on your blog or podcast or whatever platform you're using. You want people to know what you stand for and what you're all about. And also, it's really important to be active and engaged in the community. So if you're not just talking at people but actually listening and responding to comments and questions, that can go a long way.

[2:41] Brett Krock: That makes sense. What are some of your favorite resources for staying up-to-date on real estate investing? And what do you think is the most valuable resource or tool out there?

[2:50] Andrew Serious: Well, I love BiggerPockets. It's been an incredible platform for me to learn from and connect with other investors. I also read a lot of books by successful real estate investors, like Rich Dad, Poor Dad, The Millionaire Real Estate Investor, and The Bigger Picture. And then there are also great podcasts out there, like Your Money or Your Life and The Value Investing Real Estate Podcast.

[3:15] Brett Krock: Great recommendations. What would be your advice for someone who is just starting their real estate investing journey? How can they get involved in the community and network effectively without asking for value upfront?

[3:28] Andrew Serious: I think one of the best ways to get started is by serving others first, whether that's by sharing your knowledge through a blog or social media presence, volunteering with a local real estate group, or just being helpful in other ways. And then as you build up credibility and trust within the community, people will start approaching you for advice or guidance.

[3:48] Brett Krock: That's fantastic advice. What are some of the challenges that you've faced in your real estate investing journey so far? And how have you overcome them?

[3:56] Andrew Serious: One big challenge we've faced is staying focused and avoiding shiny object syndrome, which can distract from our long-term goals. Another challenge has been navigating the market and finding deals that make sense given where we are financially and what we want to achieve. But through consistent effort and a clear plan, we've been able to overcome these challenges.

[4:16] Brett Krock: I think those are great lessons for our audience to hear. What's next on the horizon for you and Stewardship Properties?

[4:23] Andrew Serious: Well, we're continuing to grow and expand, both in terms of the number of deals we're working on and the types of properties we're interested in. We have a new division coming soon that will focus more on larger multifamily assets, but for now, our focus is still on houses and small multis.

[4:39] Brett Krock: And finally, what's one thing you wish your younger self knew when starting out with real estate investing?

[4:46] Andrew Serious: I think I would have benefited from being more aggressive in pursuing opportunities and less worried about making mistakes. It can be scary to take risks, but the rewards often outweigh the potential downsides.

[4:59] Brett Krock: Great advice. All right, thanks so much for joining us today, Andrew. Where can people find you online if they want to learn more about your work or get in touch with you?

[5:07] Andrew Serious: You can check out my blog at biggerpockets.com and my personal site at andrewserious.com. And of course, we have the Good Stewards Podcast on all major platforms.

[5:16] Brett Krock: Great. Well, thanks again for joining us today and sharing your insights with our audience. We appreciate it so much. Take care.

title: Mariners Prospects, A-Rod, Griffey Jr., and More

podcastTranscript.text: Hey there, baseball fans. Welcome to another episode of The SABRmetric Edge Podcast, where we discuss all things related to baseball analytics and the Seattle Mariners. Today, we're going to dive into some topics like Mariners prospects, A-Rod, Ken Griffey Jr., and more.

We've got a lot of great questions from our listeners, so let's get started with the first one. Daniel Hardrove wants to know if we have any thoughts on the Mariners' prospects and how they're shaping up.
Andrew, what are your thoughts on the current state of the Mariners' prospect pool?

Well, I think the Mariners have some promising prospects. Jared Kelenoid is one of them. He's a shortstop who has drawn comparisons to other great players in that position like Carlos Correa and Francisco Lindor. Another prospect worth mentioning is Kyle Lewis, who played his first full season at the major league level last year. He showed flashes of brilliance with both the bat and the glove.
Great points, Andrew. We also have a question from Francis asking about the salary cap in baseball. Is there really no salary cap? Can teams spend as much money as they want on players?

That's a great question, Francis. There is no formal salary cap in Major League Baseball. However, the league has implemented various rules and guidelines to prevent teams from spending too much money. For instance, there are luxury tax penalties for exceeding certain payroll thresholds. These measures help ensure financial stability within the league.
Moving on to another topic, we have a listener asking about Albert Pujols and whether he would be a good fit for the Mariners. What do you think, Justin?

Albert Pujols is definitely an intriguing option for any team looking to improve their offense. While it's hard to predict how he would perform with the Mariners, his experience and leadership could be valuable assets. However, given his age and contract situation, I think it might be more realistic to focus on developing younger players like Kelenoid and Lewis.

Got it. Speaking of player development, we have a question about the Mariners' farm system. How important is it for teams to develop their own talent rather than relying solely on free agency or trades?

Developing your own talent can be crucial in building a successful organization, Andrew. It allows teams to control player contracts and create depth within their system. The Mariners have made some progress in this area over the past few years, but there's always room for improvement.
We also received a question about the Seattle Mariners' history with Hall of Fame players. What are your thoughts on Ken Griffey Jr.'s departure from the team in 1998?

Ken Griffey Jr.'s decision to leave the Mariners was indeed controversial at the time. While his personal reasons for moving on were understandable, it's difficult not to feel nostalgic about watching one of the greatest players in baseball history don a Mariners uniform. The team certainly lost a lot by trading him to the Cincinnati Reds.
Another question we received was about how A-Rod (Alex Rodriguez) affected the Mariners during his time with the Rangers. Do you think he helped or hindered them?

I don't believe A-Rod had a significant impact on the Mariners when they acquired him from the Rangers in 2014. By that point, the team was already struggling, and bringing in a high-priced player who wasn't performing well didn't help matters. His departure in 2015 allowed the organization to focus on rebuilding rather than dealing with a contract situation.
Lastly, we have a question about Randy Johnson and whether he would be a better fit for the Mariners now compared to when he played in Seattle. What are your thoughts, Justin?

Randy Johnson was an incredible pitcher who had success with the Mariners during his first stint from 1995-2002. While he's still a dominant player at that time, it's hard to imagine him being as effective now due to advancements in pitching mechanics and analytics. The Mariners would likely be better served by focusing on developing younger arms who can keep up with the current pace of the game.

That's all the time we have for today, folks. Thank you to everyone who submitted questions and comments. We hope you enjoyed this episode of The SABRmetric Edge Podcast, and we'll see you next time with more baseball analysis and insights.

title: Discussing Racism and Police Brutality with a Friend
summary: In this episode, we dive into the difficult topic of racism and police brutality in America. Our guest shares personal reflections and insights from their experiences as a black individual in America. They discuss the importance of allowing people to process grief and trauma, checking on friends who may be experiencing heightened emotions during these times, and offering forgiveness even when it feels hard. The conversation also touches on the impact social media has on amplifying and spreading awareness about these issues.
transcript: {host} You're listening to ‘Life’s a Story’, your go-to source for meaningful conversations that inspire change in your life and the lives of those around you.

{host} I'm [Host Name], and today we have a very heavy but necessary topic to discuss. We are joined by a dear friend, [Friend's Name], who has been at the forefront of understanding social justice issues, particularly those related to racism and police brutality in America. Welcome to the show, [Friend's Name].
[Friend's Name] Thank you for having me. I'm excited to have this conversation.

{host} Of course, we were devastated by what happened with George Floyd a few weeks ago. It was a dark day for so many of us who are tired of seeing the same cycle play out time and time again. We're going to be honest, it’s in Georgia, which makes it even worse because I think about all my friends that could have been his. What can we do? How can we help?
[Friend's Name] Thank you for coming to me. I was the first person who came to your mind and I appreciate that. It’s a difficult topic but one that needs to be discussed.
{host} Absolutely, so how did all of this begin for you? What were your initial thoughts when you saw those videos from a few weeks ago?

[Friend's Name] Well, it was just as devastating as it is for everyone else. I’ve been living with the knowledge that something like this could happen to someone I love or even to me. The reality of it is gut-wrenching.
{host} Can you tell us a bit more about your perspective on the situation and what we, as individuals and as a society, can do?

[Friend's Name] Absolutely. Firstly, allowing people to have time to grieve and process everything that’s been going on is crucial. We see these videos initially and it’s shocking, but then when they’re constantly reposted on social media, it can turn into PTSD. It’s important to check in with your friends who are minorities, especially during times like this.
{host} That's such an important point. I never thought about it that way before. Can you elaborate on why checking in is so vital?

[Friend's Name] When the trauma becomes normalized and we’re constantly reminded of these incidents, it can be incredibly draining. Just reaching out to a friend and saying 'Hey, are you okay?' or ‘Do you need anything?’ can provide immense relief. It shows that you care about their well-being and understand what they're going through.
{host} That’s beautiful. And I appreciate the advice, I’m definitely going to do that moving forward. Thank you for being here today and sharing your thoughts with us.

[Friend's Name] You’re very welcome. And remember, it’s okay to be angry, to feel hurt, but also to offer forgiveness in a way that shows you are not contributing to the problem. We need to keep spreading awareness without causing further trauma.
{host} Absolutely. It truly breaks my heart when I think about all of this and what we’re going through as a society. Thank you for being on here today, [Friend's Name].
[Friend's Name] You're very welcome, [Host Name]. Thank you for having me.
conclusion: {host} We hope that this conversation has shed some light on these important issues and inspired us all to take action. Remember, we are one humanity and it’s in our power to make a difference. If you enjoyed today’s episode, please share it with your friends and family. And as always, thank you for being here.

title: Dick Epps - Leadership, Stewardship, and Strategic Planning
transcript:
HOST:  You're listening to the Information Playground on WVLP. I'm Ron Bush with RonBush Consulting.com. Dick Epps is a friend of mine from Moody Bible Institute. He now works for his own business called Next Consulting. Today we are going to talk about leadership, stewardship and strategic planning.

HOST:  We have been in contact over the last few months and he's been growing this beard out and I think it looks really good on him. Is that a DL Moody lookalike? Are you moving to France?

GUEST:  I figured I'd let it grow until the CO. Longer. You remember, if people listening may or may not know the whole Moody thing, DL Moody was a very big man. And he made a big difference in Chicago and he had a long beard. And we used to not allow beards at Moody, you know, for employees. And so I used to say, well, I have a beard because it was a DL Moody lookalike contest. Then I started thinking about how portly he was. And I don't like that idea anymore.

HOST:  Well, hopefully, hopefully it will get too much longer. It's been fun catching up and talking to you again, Dick. What are some of the key points in your leadership process with the three faces of a pyramid?

GUEST:  Okay, let me just run through the three phases of the pyramid. The first is people. Key element is round peg into a round hole. Get the right person for the job and that's based on performance, attitude, all kinds of things. Back to the process of greenness for go, help them get 60 to 70% of their greens in their job. Then you have your leader as called and committed. You basically want people playing their positions well. We couldn't afford the wrong person in the wrong spot at Moody because it messed everything up.

HOST:  The second face is planning, key person there for me has been Bob Beal with his book 'Master Planning'. Then on the funding side, you have Ray Line and his ministry called Lifestyle Giving, who gave a job description of five circles. Acquisition, response, cultivation, vision leader, partnership, vision funding, legacy.

GUEST:  People don't take there's no U-hall on the back of the hearse. Basically everybody is either going to leave it or they have a plan for it and if you haven't addressed that in what you're trying to accomplish with your mission then you're leaving opportunity on the table.

HOST:  Excellent, Dick. Well, I've enjoyed our time together. It's been surprising how much beer you've had to drink while we were talking but it's kind of like Francis Schaeffer said, 'I don't think God wants his people to be afraid to get a little drunk on the Spirit'. Do you have any final thoughts for us?

GUEST:  I hit them real quick, hit and run, but basically, just like a good sermon has three points in a palm, a good development plan or stewardship plan has a very systematic process in order to get it done. Some of it's science, the return on investment issue is very obvious. Just do the study on what you spend in order to get a return on that investment. But it's also the fact that you have this element of how do you fit into the total organization and all these. So you can have a good plan, there's a science of it, and then there's the art of it. And then there's the business of it.

HOST:  Dick, thank you for being with us today on the Information Playground and I want to thank everyone for listening and watching. You've been listening to the information playground broadcast on WVLP that’s wvlp.org if you're streaming or it's 103.1 on the FM dial if you're in Valparaiso, Indiana. You can catch us there on Monday mornings at 8 a.m. And Friday afternoons at 1 p.m. Or you can catch us on demand at any of the podcast platforms just look for the information playground. The definitive article or the definite article is important. The information playground. Apparently that's a popular name. And you can catch us there or you can catch us on YouTube with the same channel name. I hope everyone stays safe and healthy.
